findings.title: Printed transport coupling reverses the Brownian sign
findings.assertion_status: Theorem 8.1 is false for the printed same-Brownian-path scheme.
findings.hypotheses: d=1, b=bn=0, p=q=p1=q1=4, nu=0, l=2, rbar=8, rho(x)=exp(-(x-1)^2). Zero drift satisfies Condition B, and all three strict parameter conditions hold. rho belongs to every required W1r.
findings.evidence: From (8.3), the reversed driver is W_(tau-s)-W_tau, while (8.4)-(8.5) use its negative. Exact u=rho(x-Wt), printed un=rho(x+Wt). At t=1,x=0 the squared L2 error is 2/sqrt(5)*(exp(-2/5)-exp(-2))>0, independent of n. Actual Sympy calculation gives L2=0.6917404994780121.
findings.counterevidence: The opposite drivers have the same marginal Brownian law, but that does not identify the strong coupling on which (8.6) is based.
findings.core_dependency: Inverse-flow construction and Theorem 8.1, not the main SDE theorem.
findings.repair_impact: Reverse the definition of W^tau and its extension (8.7). This removes the exhibited obstruction; no assertion of an independently accepted corrected theorem.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Major: the printed scheme in Theorem 8.1 does not converge to the stated solution]
Equations (8.3)--(8.5), pp.~47--48, change the sign of the Brownian increment while retaining the same driving path. Consequently the strong estimate (8.6) is false for the printed scheme.
\end{problem}
\begin{proof}
The definition \(X_s^\tau=X_{\tau,\tau-s}\) and (8.3) give
\[
X_s^\tau=x-\int_0^s b(\tau-r,X_r^\tau)\,dr+W_{\tau-s}-W_\tau.
\]
The paper instead uses a plus sign before \(W_s^\tau=W_\tau-W_{\tau-s}\), in both (8.4) and the numerical scheme (8.5).

Take \(d=1\), \(b=b^n=0\), \(p=q=p_1=q_1=4\), \(\nu=0\), \(l=2\), and \(\bar r=8\). Then all restrictions in Theorem 8.1 hold: \(1/4+2/4<1\), \(\nu<7/8\), and \(1/8<1/2-1/4\). Zero drift satisfies Condition B with, for example, \(\mu_n(s,t)=t-s\) and any fixed positive \(\theta\). Set
\(\rho(x)=e^{-(x-1)^2}\), which belongs to every required \(W^{1,r}\) space. The Stratonovich chain rule gives the exact solution
\(u(t,x)=\rho(x-W_t)\).
The printed scheme gives \(u^n(t,x)=\rho(x+W_t)\) for every \(n\).
For \(Z=W_1\sim N(0,1)\), direct Gaussian integration yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transport}
\E|\rho(Z)-\rho(-Z)|^2
=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}\left(e^{-2/5}-e^{-2}\right)>0.
\end{equation}
The corresponding \(L^2\) error is approximately \(0.6917405\).
At \((t,x)=(1,0)\), the left side of (8.6) is therefore bounded away from zero, while its right side tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\).
\end{proof}
\emph{Counterevidence and repair.}
Both signs of a Brownian motion have the same marginal law. This does not repair an estimate of the difference of two solutions coupled to the same \(W\). Defining the reversed driver as \(W_{\tau-s}-W_\tau\), with the corresponding change to its extension (8.7), repairs this elementary sign obstruction. The issue concerns the stated transport algorithm and Theorem 8.1; it does not contradict the earlier SDE rate. The same signs occur on v6 pp.~54--55.

\section{Uniform localization in the appendix}

findings.title: Uniform-in-time Sobolev localization smallness is false
findings.source_locator: Condition A' printed p.50; Lemma A.8/A.19 pp.52-53; A.9 pp.53-54; A.10 p.55; A.5/A.11 pp.51,56-57.
findings.assertion_status: False Lemma A.8; invalid central PDE derivation; final PDE/SDE statements not disproved.
findings.hypotheses: d=1, p0=4, p=2, q=4; f=g=0. rj=2^-j, phi=(1-u^2)^2 on [-1,1] and zero outside; a=2+rj^(3/4)phi(x/rj) on disjoint positive-length time intervals (2^(-j-1),2^-j]. Else a=2. Measurable, 2<=a<=3, weak derivative uniformly bounded in L4, and 1/p+1/p0<1.
findings.evidence: Gradient L4 norm^4 is 65536/15015 for every j. For a smooth cutoff equal to one near zero, rho_j=4rj and z=0, the derivative of (a-a(z))*cutoff equals the bump derivative on its support. Its L4 norm is bounded below by the same positive constant. Thus the supremum (even essential in time) does not tend to zero.
findings.counterevidence: Absolute continuity gives this smallness for one fixed gradient and fixed time; it does not give uniformity over a bounded family of Lp functions.
findings.core_dependency: A.8 -> A.9 Step1/absorption -> A.10 -> A.5/A.11 -> Proposition 6.4 -> weak-topology part of Theorem 2.3.
findings.repair_impact: Add uniform local equiintegrability of the gradient family, or supply a different argument under the original assumptions. Neither is supplied by the printed L-infinity-in-time norm bound.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Major: Lemma A.8 requires uniform local integrability not supplied by Condition A']
Lemma A.8, (A.19), p.~52, asserts that
\[
\sup_{t,z}\|(a-a(z))\psi_\rho^z\|_{W^{1,p_0}}\longrightarrow0
\quad(\rho\downarrow0)
\]
from the bound \(\sup_t\|\nabla a(t)\|_{p_0}<\infty\). This assertion is false.
\end{problem}
\begin{proof}
Use \(d=1\), \(p_0=4\), \(p=2\), \(q=4\), and zero forcing terms, so that \(p_0>d\) and \(1/p+1/p_0<1\).
Let \(r_j=2^{-j}\) and \(\phi(u)=(1-u^2)^2\) on \([-1,1]\), zero outside. This compactly supported \(C^1\) function is sufficient for the weak differentiability required in Condition A'. On the disjoint intervals
\(I_j=(2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]\), set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:concentration}
a(t,x)=2+r_j^{3/4}\phi(x/r_j),\qquad t\in I_j,
\end{equation}
and set \(a=2\) at all remaining times.
Then \(2\leq a\leq3\), the coefficient is measurable, and
\[
\|\partial_xa(t,\cdot)\|_4^4
=r_j^{4(3/4-1)+1}\int_{-1}^1|\phi'(u)|^4\,du
=\frac{65536}{15015}>0.
\]
Thus its gradient norm is uniformly bounded in time, exactly as required.

Choose a smooth cutoff \(\psi_1\) supported in \([-1,1]\) and identically one on \([-1/2,1/2]\). For \(\rho_j=4r_j\), \(z=0\), and \(t\in I_j\), the cutoff \(\psi_{\rho_j}^0\) is identically one on the support of the bump. The average \(a(0)\) in the paper is spatially constant. Consequently
\[
\|\partial_x[(a-a(0))\psi_{\rho_j}^0]\|_4
\geq \|\partial_xa\|_{L^4([-r_j,r_j])}
=\|\phi'\|_4>0.
\]
The asserted limit fails, also with essential supremum in time because every \(I_j\) has positive measure. Equivalence of Bessel and classical first-order Sobolev norms gives the same contradiction in the paper's notation.
\end{proof}
\emph{Dependency and impact.}
The false smallness is used in Lemma A.9, Step 1, p.~53, and absorbed in Step 2, p.~54. Lemma A.10 repeats that argument; Theorems A.5 and A.11 then feed Proposition 6.4 and the weak-topology estimates of Theorem 2.3. This is an invalid central derivation, not a demonstrated counterexample to those final PDE or SDE estimates.

\emph{Counterevidence and repair boundary.}
For a single time-independent gradient in \(L^{p_0}\), absolute continuity of its integral does give the needed local smallness uniformly over spatial centers. The missing point is uniformity over the time-indexed family. A uniform local equiintegrability assumption, such as
\(\sup_{t,z}\int_{B_\rho(z)}|\nabla a(t,x)|^{p_0}\,dx\to0\),
would support this step. Alternatively the localization proof must be replaced. Neither repair follows from the stated norm bound alone. The same assertion and inference occur as Lemma .8 on v6 pp.~59--60.

\section{The principal strong-error derivation}

findings.title: Strong-error proof drops diffusion forcing and uses an unprovided sigma regularity
findings.source_locator: Condition A1 pp.4-5; Proposition 7.3, (7.6)-(7.7), printed pp.42-44.
findings.assertion_status: False intermediate (7.7) and invalid proof dependencies; Theorem 2.2 not disproved.
findings.hypotheses: First example: d=1, b=bn=0, U=0, x0=x0n=0, sigma=1+tanh(x)/4, n=1, p=q=p0=4, q0=infinity, pbar=2, alpha=1. Smooth bounded uniformly elliptic Lipschitz sigma and integrable gradient satisfy all conditions. Separate regularity example: d=2, p=q=8, p0=4, q0=infinity, b=bn=0, sigma a rotation of angle cutoff*|x|^(3/4), a=I, alpha=1.
findings.evidence: All terms of printed V vanish in the first example, but one-step Euler is B and the exact nonconstant-diffusion SDE cannot be B by Ito isometry. Weighted error is positive, contradicting (7.7). Moment bounds cannot replace a random increment integral by a deterministic value. In the second example covariance is constant but sigma is not Lipschitz, while its gradient is L4. Also Ito's formula requires 1/2 times Hessian U at Xn, not Hessian at X, in the covariance correction.
findings.counterevidence: The final claimed rate contains a diffusion-error contribution; abstract language suggests sigma Holder regularity may have been intended. Neither observation validates the printed intermediate estimate.
findings.core_dependency: Zvonkin-transformed Euler error, stochastic Gronwall estimate and exponential-weight removal in main Theorem 2.2.
findings.repair_impact: Retain a nondecreasing random diffusion forcing with the required moment bound; specify sigma regularity or prove another estimate; correct Hessian location/factor and justify the discrete-path occupation estimate.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Major: the diffusion forcing is lost in Proposition 7.3]
The proof on pp.~42--44 contains a false intermediate conclusion (7.7), as well as a use of \(\alpha\)-H\"older regularity of \(\sigma\) which is not implied by Condition A1.
\end{problem}
\begin{proof}[Decisive check of (7.7)]
In the paper, \(V=|x_0-x_0^n|^{\bar p}+V^1+V^2+V^3\).
Take \(d=1\), \(b=b^n=0\), \(x_0=x_0^n=0\), and
\[
\sigma(x)=1+\tfrac14\tanh x.
\]
This coefficient is smooth, bounded, uniformly elliptic and Lipschitz; its derivative belongs to every finite \(L^{p_0}\). Take \(p=q=p_0=4\), \(q_0=\infty\), \(\bar p=2\), and \(\alpha=1\). The assumptions hold. The PDE solution \(U\) is zero, so every term in the displayed \(V\) is zero.

For \(n=1\), the Euler process is \(X_t^1=B_t\), whereas the exact solution satisfies \(dX_t=\sigma(X_t)dB_t\). These paths cannot agree almost surely throughout \([0,1]\): equality would imply, by It\^o isometry,
\(\E\int_0^1(\sigma(B_s)-1)^2ds=0\), which is false. Thus
\(\E\sup_t|X_t-X_t^1|^2>0\).
The weight in (7.7) is strictly positive and bounded away from zero here, since \(\nabla\sigma\) and its maximal function are bounded. The claimed bound
\[
\E e^{-c_{\bar p}|A_1^n|^{\max(\bar p/2,1)}}\xi_1\leq \E V_1=0
\]
is impossible.
\end{proof}

The preceding estimate of \(I^2\) on p.~44 replaces a random increment integral by a deterministic \(n^{-\bar p\alpha/2}\) using Lemma 7.2, which is only a moment estimate. Even for \(X^n=B\), \(\int_0^{1/n}|B_r|^2dr\) is not deterministically bounded by a fixed multiple of \(n^{-1}\). A random nondecreasing error term must remain in \(V\), with its expectation bounded at the required rate; the paper's definition of \(V\) omits it.

There is also a separate hypothesis mismatch at that step. In \(d=2\), let \(\vartheta(x)=\chi(x)|x|^{3/4}\), with a smooth cutoff equal to one near zero, and let \(\sigma(x)\) be planar rotation by angle \(\vartheta(x)\). Then
\[
\sigma\sigma^*=I,\qquad \nabla\sigma\in L^4(\R^2),\qquad
\frac{\|\sigma(re_1)-\sigma(0)\|_{\rm HS}}r
=\frac{\sqrt8|\sin(r^{3/4}/2)|}r\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
The gradient is integrable to the fourth power near zero because its radial integral is proportional to \(\int_0^1 r^{4(-1/4)}r\,dr\).
With \(p=q=8\), \(p_0=4\), \(q_0=\infty\), and zero drifts, all formal assumptions hold with \(\alpha=1\), but \(\sigma\) is not Lipschitz. Thus H\"older regularity of \(a\) cannot simply be substituted for the same regularity of \(\sigma\).

Finally, the covariance correction in (7.6) must be
\[
\frac12\int_0^t\nabla^2U(r,X_r^n):
 [a(r,X_{k_n(r)}^n)-a(r,X_r^n)]\,dr.
\]
The printed formula uses \(X_r\) and omits \(1/2\); It\^o's formula for \(U(t,X_t^n)\) evaluates its Hessian at \(X_t^n\). Its subsequent estimate therefore needs a discrete-path occupation estimate.

\emph{Counterevidence and repair boundary.}
The abstract describes the diffusion coefficient itself as H\"older continuous, which may reflect the intended hypothesis; the formal Condition A1 controls its covariance instead. Explicitly strengthening that condition and retaining the random diffusion forcing would address two identified obstacles. The existing strong-rate statement includes a diffusion-error term, so the counterexample to (7.7) does not refute Theorem 2.2. These proof passages persist on v6 pp.~48--51.

\section{Further local errors with explicit repairs}

findings.title: Gaussian difference bound uses an impossibly narrow envelope
findings.source_locator: Lemma 3.11/(3.22), printed p.16; explicit variance conventions pp.2,17; use in Lemma 5.2 p.25.
findings.assertion_status: False local density bound, with a standard wider-envelope repair.
findings.hypotheses: d=1, positive scalar covariances Sigma=1 and barSigma=2, K=2, satisfying the lemma's comparability assumptions.
findings.evidence: |p1-p2| / (0.5*(p_(1/2)+p1)) is asymptotic to sqrt(2)*exp(x^2/4), so no N(d,K) works. Analytic tail calculation and independent numerical evaluations retained.
findings.counterevidence: Precision-matrix notation would change the direction, but the source explicitly uses variance/covariance notation.
findings.core_dependency: Kernel regularity estimates in Lemma 5.2 and subsequent discrete smoothing argument.
findings.repair_impact: Use wider covariance Gaussian envelopes by differentiation/interpolation and absorption of polynomial factors. This changes constants rather than the required time powers.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Minor: the Gaussian envelope in Lemma 3.11 has the wrong width]
Equation (3.22), p.~16, bounds a difference of Gaussian densities by densities with half the covariance. It is false even in dimension one with positive covariances.
\end{problem}
For \(\Sigma=1,\bar\Sigma=2,K=2\), all its scalar comparison hypotheses hold. With the paper's variance convention,
\[
\frac{|p_1(x)-p_2(x)|}{|1-1/2|\,[p_{1/2}(x)+p_1(x)]}
\sim \sqrt2\,e^{x^2/4}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
No constant \(N(d,K)\) can work. The proof of Lemma 5.2 on p.~25 and later uses of Lemma 3.11 inherit this invalid envelope.
Wider Gaussian envelopes, obtained by differentiating the density along a covariance interpolation and absorbing its quadratic polynomial into a slower Gaussian, give the required type of estimate. This changes constants and Gaussian widths, not the displayed time exponents in (5.5)--(5.6). That local repair is why this is classified Minor. A precision-matrix interpretation is incompatible with the explicit variance convention on p.~2 and the density formula on p.~17. The same half-covariance envelope appears on v6 pp.~19 and 28.

findings.title: Covariance and Duhamel factors are inconsistent
findings.source_locator: (5.3)-(5.4), printed p.23; H definition p.23; (5.10), p.26.
findings.assertion_status: False printed kernel representation and Duhamel normalization; final smoothing rate not disproved.
findings.hypotheses: First test sigma=1, f=cos(x). Second test d=1, smooth a=1+exp(-x^2)/2, sigma=sqrt(a), f=1, s=0, 0<t<1/n. These are smooth bounded uniformly elliptic admissible coefficients.
findings.evidence: Actual covariance is integral a, while printed Sigma is half that. Constant sigma gives exp(-t/2)cos(x) versus exp(-t/4)cos(x). For f=1, Q1=1, T1=1+(t/2)a''+o(t), integral QH1=-t a''+o(t); the printed RHS is 1+t/2+o(t) at x=0.
findings.counterevidence: A uniform covariance convention cannot reconcile both the actual random variable in (5.3) and the printed factors.
findings.core_dependency: Discrete Duhamel formula and kernel estimates.
findings.repair_impact: Use Sigma=integral a, generator (1/2)a:D2, and (1/2)H. The scalar factors can be carried through constants.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Minor: inconsistent covariance and generator normalizations in Section 5]
Equations (5.3)--(5.4), p.~23, and the Duhamel identity (5.10), p.~26, do not use a consistent factor \(1/2\).
\end{problem}
The random variable in (5.3) has covariance
\(\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\), whereas (5.4) prints
\(\Sigma_{s,t}=\frac12\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\).
For constant \(\sigma=1\) and \(f(x)=\cos x\), the actual adjoint in (5.3) gives
\(e^{-(t-s)/2}\cos x\); the printed kernel gives
\(e^{-(t-s)/4}\cos x\).

Even if \(T\) is defined by the actual adjoint (5.3), the \(H\) defined on p.~23 needs a factor \(1/2\) in (5.10). To see this without a convention ambiguity, take smooth time-independent
\(a(x)=1+\frac12e^{-x^2}\), \(f=1\), \(s=0\), and \(0<t<1/n\).
Then \(Q_{0,t}^n1=1\), while the actual adjoint has
\(T_{0,t}1=1+\frac t2a''+o(t)\) and
\(\int_0^tQ_{0,k_n(r)}^nH_{r,t}^n1\,dr=-ta''+o(t)\).
At \(x=0\), the printed right side of (5.10) is \(1+t/2+o(t)\), not 1.

A consistent repair uses \(\Sigma=\int a\), the generator \(\frac12a^{ij}\partial_{ij}\), and \(\frac12H\) in the Duhamel formula. These factors can be absorbed in the subsequent norm estimates; the smoothing-rate conclusion is not refuted. The same definitions and (5.10) occur on v6 pp.~26--29.

findings.title: Proposition 4.6(b) has the wrong control power
findings.source_locator: Proposition 4.6(a)-(b), printed pp.21-22; correct downstream powers in Theorem 6.1(iii) and 2.3(iii).
findings.assertion_status: False local homogeneity; downstream displayed rates already use the repair.
findings.hypotheses: d=1,p=q=4,pbar=1, g_epsilon=epsilon*f, f smooth compactly supported nonnegative nonzero with L4 norm one; w0(s,t)=epsilon^4(t-s), Gamma=1. Bessel potential order -1 is an L4 contraction.
findings.evidence: The left side is c*epsilon with c>0, but printed right side N*w0(0,1) is N*epsilon^4. This fails as epsilon tends to zero.
findings.counterevidence: Part(a), Theorem6.1(iii), and Theorem2.3(iii) already print w0^(1/q).
findings.core_dependency: Continuum occupation bounds for weak drift discrepancies.
findings.repair_impact: Replace w0 by w0^(1/q) in part(b); no final convergence theorem is refuted.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Minor: Proposition 4.6(b) has incorrect homogeneity]
The right side on p.~21 contains \(w_0(0,1)\), whereas it must scale as \(w_0(0,1)^{1/q}\).
\end{problem}
Take \(d=1,p=q=4,\bar p=1\). Let \(f\geq0\) be smooth, nonzero, compactly supported and normalized by \(\|f\|_4=1\). Put \(g_\epsilon(t,x)=\epsilon f(x)\), \(w_0(s,t)=\epsilon^4(t-s)\), and \(\Gamma=1\).
The Bessel potential operator of order \(-1\) is an \(L^4\) contraction, so both hypotheses of Proposition 4.6 hold. Its left side equals
\(\epsilon\,\E\int_0^1 f(B_r)dr=c\epsilon\), with \(c>0\), whereas its right side is \(N\epsilon^4\). This fails as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\).
Part (a) already has the correct power; Theorem 6.1(iii) and Theorem 2.3(iii) also print the correct power. Restoring it in part (b) repairs this localized statement. It does not establish a defect in their final rate. The same incorrect power is visible on v6 p.~24.

findings.title: Girsanov density uses the wrong direction/process
findings.source_locator: (5.33) and following law claim, printed pp.36-37; continuum argument p.40.
findings.assertion_status: Incorrect change-of-measure law identity, locally repairable.
findings.hypotheses: Take sigma=1 and smooth compactly supported bn=b equal to one near the initial point; all drift integrability/local boundedness assumptions hold. Density is exp(-integral u dB -1/2 integral |u|2).
findings.evidence: Under Q=rho P, Btilde=B+integral u is Brownian. Hence the driftless Euler process has drift -bn under Q, not +bn as claimed. Their initial generators differ.
findings.counterevidence: One can consistently start from the drifted process with the negative density, or from the driftless process with the positive density. The printed process/direction choice does neither.
findings.core_dependency: Girsanov transfer of discrete and continuum occupation estimates.
findings.repair_impact: Use the positive stochastic-integral sign for driftless-to-positive-drift transfer or consistently reverse the process. The |u|2 moment estimates survive. No v6 comparison of these passages is asserted.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Minor: the change-of-measure direction in (5.33) is reversed]
The density in the proof of Theorem 5.1, p.~36, introduces the negative of the desired drift into the driftless Euler process.
\end{problem}
Let \(u_r=(\sigma^{-1}b^n)(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)\) and use the printed density
\(\rho=\exp(-\int u\,dB-\frac12\int|u|^2dr)\).
Under \(dQ=\rho\,dP\), \(\widetilde B=B+\int u\,dr\) is Brownian. Hence
\[
d\bar X_r^n
=\sigma(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)d\widetilde B_r
-b^n(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)dr,
\]
rather than the positive drift in (1.3). This distinction already occurs for a smooth compactly supported scalar drift equal to one near the initial point, which satisfies Condition B. The two laws have opposite initial drift generators.

Use the positive stochastic-integral sign to obtain the positive drift under the new measure. The exponential-moment argument depends on \(|u|^2\), so its estimates survive this correction. The continuum proof on p.~40 similarly evaluates its negative-sign density along \(\bar X\) while making a claim about the law of \(X\); it must consistently choose the process and direction of measure change. These are repairable proof identities, not counterexamples to the stated moment estimates. No independent comparison of these two passages with v6 is asserted here.

findings.title: Negative-order multiplier norm is used in place of positive order
findings.source_locator: Theorem2.3(iii) proof, printed p.46; Lemma A.3 p.50; regularity (7.2) p.41.
findings.assertion_status: False displayed product bound and inconsistent temporal exponent choice, locally repairable.
findings.hypotheses: d=1,p=2,q=10 satisfies d/p+4/q<1. For smooth compactly supported nonzero psi, gk=hk=psi cos(kx), constant in time.
findings.evidence: Both H^-1 norms are O(1/k), while product tends in H^-1 to psi^2/2. Thus two negative-order factors cannot obey the printed multiplier inequality.
findings.counterevidence: The actual g=grad U has the positive-order Lq_t L^(1,p)_x bound by (7.2), with p>d.
findings.core_dependency: Product drift discrepancy bound for Theorem2.3(iii).
findings.repair_impact: Use positive-order norm for g and choose q2=q to give q3=q/2. Final (2.11) is not disproved.
findings.proof_tex_excerpt:
\begin{problem}[Minor: the multiplier norm in Theorem 2.3(iii)'s proof has the wrong order]
On p.~46, the product estimate and the definition of \(w_1\) use \(\|g\|_{L^q_tL^{-1,p}_x}\), although Lemma A.3 requires the multiplier in the positive-order space \(L^{1,p}\).
\end{problem}
There is no continuous multiplication map \(H^{-1}(\R)\times H^{-1}(\R)\to H^{-1}(\R)\).
For a nonzero smooth compactly supported \(\psi\), take \(g_k=h_k=\psi(x)\cos(kx)\). Both \(H^{-1}\) norms are \(O(k^{-1})\), while
\[
g_kh_k=\tfrac12\psi^2+\tfrac12\psi^2\cos(2kx)
\longrightarrow\tfrac12\psi^2\ne0\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1}.
\]
Thus the printed negative-order product bound fails. This check applies already with \(d=1,p=2,q=10\), which obey \(d/p+4/q<1\); a constant time dependence supplies the temporal norms.

Here \(g=\nabla U\) actually has a uniformly bounded \(L^q_tL^{1,p}_x\) norm by (7.2), and \(p>d\). Replacing the negative-order norm of \(g\) by the positive-order norm repairs the multiplication step. The sentence choosing \(q_2=2\) must also be made consistent with \(q_3=q/2\): the available choice is \(q_2=q\). With these repairs, the product control has the required homogeneity. This local error does not refute (2.11). The same multiplier sign occurs on v6 p.~53.

independent_acceptance_checks.method: Focused manual analytic rederivation against decisive source passages and counterevidence; original calculation receipts reused where matching, not rerun or reattributed.

problems.assumptions_checked: d=1;p=q=p1=q1=4;nu=0;l=2;rbar=8;rho smooth rapidly decaying;Condition B holds with positive fixed bounds.
problems.counterevidence_boundary: Brownian marginal symmetry does not validate the same-path strong estimate. Earlier SDE rate not refuted.

problems.decisive_check: Read full Condition A-prime and A.19. For the prescribed positive-length time intervals the derivative scaling is r^(4*(3/4-1)+1)=1; at rho_j=4r_j the cutoff is flat on the bump, so its W1,4 norm has a fixed positive lower bound. The spatial average has zero derivative.
